abstract: This study analyzes TV audience participation on Twitter across an entire 2012-2013 season of two Italian shows from different genres: the talent show The X Factor and the political talk show Servizio Pubblico. Using a dataset of 1,383,414 tweets, the authors apply a peak-detection algorithm to identify moments of heightened online engagement and link them to the corresponding broadcast scenes. A content analysis of over 12,000 tweets from engagement peaks reveals how audiences' willingness to express opinions differs when discussing politics versus entertainment, with political discussion showing more indirect, information-backed, and joke-framed expression.
key_claims: Full-season, cross-genre analysis of social TV reveals both genre-dependent and genre-independent audience behaviors that episode- or event-focused studies miss.

Surprise and suspense are the key 'typical selectors' that catalyze online audience engagement, but they operate differently across genres: talent shows use both, while political talk shows rely mainly on surprise.
Twitter engagement rhythm is closely synchronized with the structure of the TV format and producers' strategies, indicating a prevailing framing effect of television over the online conversation.

Willingness to speak up differs by topic: original opinion tweets are more frequent for entertainment, whereas politics prompts more indirect expression through retweets, jokes, and opinions bolstered by information.
The hybridization of political talk shows with entertainment means Twitter engagement around politics tends to follow a mediatized rather than strictly political logic.
methods: Collected a complete dataset of 1,383,414 tweets via the Twitter Firehose (DiscoverText GNIP Powertrack importer) from August 30, 2012 to June 30, 2013 using official hashtags #xf6 (9 episodes) and #serviziopubblico (28 episodes).
Segmented data by air time and generated minute-by-minute time series of tweets, replies, retweets, and original tweets following Bruns & Stieglitz (2013) metrics.

Applied Marcus et al.'s (2011) peak-detection algorithm to the stream of original tweets, identifying 16 seasonal peaks for The X Factor and 39 for Servizio Pubblico, to overcome sampling limits of skewed tweet distributions.
Coded the 55 corresponding TV scenes using a codebook grounded in Luhmann's (2000) media selector criteria (surprise, suspense) plus show routine position (intercoder Krippendorff's alpha = 0.68).

Content-analyzed over 12,000 original tweets from eight sampled peaks (the two highest and two lowest original-tweet-share peaks per show) using an adapted AEIO-style matrix with categories: information, opinion, opinion as joke, emotion, attention seeking, interaction (intercoder alpha = 0.71).
findings: The X Factor audience was far more active (62,489 avg tweets/episode, 338/min) than Servizio Pubblico (16,935 avg tweets/episode, 100/min).
The X Factor engagement combined surprise (50% of peaks) and suspense (56.2%); Servizio Pubblico relied on surprise (48.7%) with little suspense (5.1%).
Most engaging moments for Servizio Pubblico were the talk/debate and Travaglio's editorial; for The X Factor they were contestant performances, judges' comments, and eliminations.
Original tweets were more frequent during entertainment (70%) than politics (63%), and when a peer-like figure (studio audience member or contestant) was on screen.

Opinions were the most frequent tweet type for both shows (62% overall), but politics drew more jokes (25% vs 11%) and more opinion-plus-information tweets (10% vs 4%), while entertainment drew far more emotional tweets (33% vs 3%).

For political discussion only, combining opinion with information was significantly more common in low-original-tweet peaks (13% vs 7%), suggesting a strategy to bolster credibility or avoid direct, risky opinion.
Explicit requests for change (interaction) were low (~11%) and only slightly lower for politics than entertainment, challenging the assumption that political shows prompt more participatory demands.
contributions: Introduces a hybrid methodological approach combining peak detection on original-tweet streams with scene-level content analysis, avoiding bias from sampling heavily skewed tweet distributions.
Provides a rare full-season, cross-genre comparison of social TV participation spanning an entire broadcast season of two distinct formats.
Operationalizes Luhmann's media selectors (surprise and suspense) as analytical tools to explain genre-specific drivers of online engagement.
Extends and refines the AEIO/content-form codebook to capture nuanced differences in willingness to speak up and forms of opinion expression between politics and entertainment.
Empirically demonstrates television's framing effect on Twitter conversation structure, nuancing prior event-focused findings that emphasized user agency and divergence.
framing: The paper situates itself within audience and social TV / second-screen studies, drawing on the network society and hybrid media system literature (Castells, Chadwick, Jenkins) and redefinitions of participation and public opinion. It engages uses-and-gratifications theory, Carpentier's conception of participation, and Luhmann's media systems theory, while responding to calls for long-term, comparative studies of TV audience behavior on Twitter.
